definition: The sheen of a fiber, yarn or fabric, produced when smooth surfaces reflect light in a concentrated, mirror-like direction instead of scattering it diffusely, which would give a matte look.
explanation: Luster depends on how light meets the fiber surface and interior. Smooth, regular surfaces send more light in one concentrated direction, producing highlights, while rough surfaces and internal interfaces scatter light in many directions and look flatter. In wool, the size and profile of cuticle scales affect surface reflection. Internal air spaces also matter: heavily medullated fibers scatter so much light that they look chalky white. Yarn twist, fabric construction and finishing then modify how the fiber's luster reads in a garment, so the same fiber can look bright in one cloth and subdued in another.
example: A class drapes two fabrics made from the same fiber under a single lamp: a satin weave with long floats and a plain weave. As each is tilted, the satin shows bright, moving highlights, while the plain weave looks flatter. Students conclude that luster is partly a property of construction, because long, parallel floats present a more continuous reflecting surface than short, frequently interlaced yarns.
caution: Luster describes appearance, not quality, softness, cleanliness or fiber content. Luster also differs from color and whiteness: a white fabric can be matte and a dark one glossy. Shine that develops on worn dark garments at elbows or seats comes from surfaces flattened by abrasion or pressing, an unwanted luster caused by use rather than a property of the original fiber.
deeper: Surface reflection follows the Fresnel relations: at a smooth interface between air and a polymer with a refractive index near 1.5, only about 4% of light reflects specularly at normal incidence, with the fraction rising toward grazing angles, and the rest enters the fiber. Inside, interfaces such as air-filled medulla cells or pigment particles scatter light diffusely. Luster therefore increases when surfaces are smooth and flat compared with the wavelength of light and decreases when roughness or internal scatterers are present. In wool, heavy medullation raises light reflection and produces a white, chalky appearance, and studies quantify cuticle scale morphology as a surface parameter. Instrumental luster is commonly assessed by goniophotometry, which compares specular with diffuse reflectance over a range of angles.
origins: The English word, spelled lustre in British usage, shares its root with the French lustre and the Italian lustro and ultimately with Latin words for light and brightness. Textile trades have long used it for the sheen of silk and of smooth, long wools. With manufactured fibers, luster became a design variable, because producers could make filaments brighter or duller through their choice of cross-section and additives.

definition: A chain-of-custody accounting model in which certified and uncertified inputs may be physically mixed, while certified claims on outputs are capped by the verified quantity of certified input.
explanation: Under mass balance, a site records how much certified material enters a process during a defined period and allocates an equivalent quantity, adjusted for conversion losses, to outgoing products that may then carry the claim. The claimed output is connected to the same production process but need not contain the certified fibers or molecules themselves. This differs from segregation, where certified material is kept physically separate, and from book-and-claim, where credits are traded without any physical link. Mass balance tends to appear where continuous processes, such as polymer or pulp production, make physical separation impractical.
example: A yarn plant runs recycled and virgin polyester chip through one continuous line. In a quarter it buys 300 tonnes of certified recycled chip and 700 tonnes of virgin chip. With a hypothetical 95 percent yield, a mass-balance model could let it assign recycled claims to about 285 tonnes of output, although every bobbin holds the same physical mixture. Under segregation it would instead need separate batches with measurable recycled content.
caution: A mass-balance claim is an accounting statement, not a description of what a particular item physically contains. A garment sold with a mass-balance recycled claim may hold little or no recycled material. Standards differ on whether mass balance is allowed at all, how long reconciliation periods may run, whether credits can move between sites, and how claims must be worded, so check the exact standard, version and claim language.
deeper: The underlying rule is a conservation check over a site boundary and a reconciliation period: claimed output must not exceed certified input multiplied by a conversion factor, with opening balances, losses and carry-over recorded. Textile Exchange's Content Claim Standard 3.0, launched in June 2021, relies on batch-level segregation for both fully certified and blended products and limits the volume reconciliation period to no more than three months. Textile Exchange separately piloted a site-level mass-balance approach in 2021, in which sites generate credits from claimed inputs that may be assigned to outputs physically connected to production, and it has published an issue paper and a policy on alternative volume reconciliation. Auditors test any such system by reconciling purchases, production yields and sales against claimed quantities.
origins: The term comes from engineering, where a mass balance applies conservation of mass to the inputs, outputs and accumulation of a defined system. Sustainability schemes borrowed it for claims accounting in commodity supply chains, such as palm oil, cocoa and forest products, where physical separation is costly. In textiles, interest has grown alongside chemical recycling and continuous polymer processes that do not suit batch segregation.
